title: Making a product ready to scale

say: Making a product ready to scale.
This is the video for module 1 of Production Scaling and Quality Assurance.
When you make ten times more, three things change. The amounts, which you can calculate.

panel.heading: Not simply ten times everything
items: Prove it with a pilot run

say: The losses, which you must measure.

panel.heading: Not simply ten times everything
items: Prove it with a pilot run

say: And the behaviour of the process. Mixing, heating and cooling take longer with more material.

panel.heading: Not simply ten times everything
items: Prove it with a pilot run

say: So in this module you work out your numbers, check how much your output varies, and prove the bigger batch with a pilot run.

panel.heading: Not simply ten times everything
items: Prove it with a pilot run

say: Cups, tins and one small sachet change from day to day. Use a digital scale that reads to 1 g, and weigh every ingredient, including liquids and eggs.

panel.heading: Weights, percentages and yield
items: Weigh everything, even eggs and water

say: Divide each weight by the total and multiply by 100. These formula percentages do not change with batch size. They are your product's identity.

panel.heading: Weights, percentages and yield
items: Weigh everything, even eggs and water

say: Yield is how much sellable product you get from what you put in. Frying and baking lose water, and some pieces break or burn, so measure it on two or three test batches. One batch can be lucky.

panel.heading: Weights, percentages and yield
items: Weigh everything, even eggs and water

say: Then measure packing loss: spillage, samples, and packs that fail the seal check.

panel.heading: Weights, percentages and yield
items: Weigh everything, even eggs and water

say: For example, Kemi in Ibadan sells chin-chin in 250 g packs. A school wants 400 packs. That is 100,000 g of finished product.

panel.heading: Kemi: 400 packs of chin-chin
items: Round up: 8 loads of 9 kg = 72 kg

say: Her packing loss is 2%, so she must make about 102,041 g.

panel.heading: Kemi: 400 packs of chin-chin
items: Round up: 8 loads of 9 kg = 72 kg

say: Her measured yield is 85%, so she needs about 120,048 g of dough.

panel.heading: Kemi: 400 packs of chin-chin
items: Round up: 8 loads of 9 kg = 72 kg

say: Her test dough weighs 1,700 g, so the multiplier is 70.6. That means 70.6 kg of flour.

panel.heading: Kemi: 400 packs of chin-chin
items: Round up: 8 loads of 9 kg = 72 kg

say: Her rented mixer takes up to 10 kg of flour, so she rounds up to 8 equal loads of 9 kg. That gives about 407 packs.
She first guessed 40 kg of flour by doubling up. The arithmetic saved the order.

panel.heading: Kemi: 400 packs of chin-chin
items: Round up: 8 loads of 9 kg = 72 kg
panel.rule: Work backwards from what the buyer receives.

say: Large quantities of hot oil are dangerous. Keep the fryer on a stable, level surface away from children, never leave it unattended, keep a lid or fire blanket near, and never pour water on burning oil.

say: No two items are exactly the same. That difference is variation, and scaling multiplies it. For example, Ruth in Oyo packs yam flour in 1 kg bags. Never below 1,000 g, and not above 1,030 g.

panel.heading: Ruth's 1 kg bags of yam flour
items: Cpk 0.74: target too close to 1,000 g

say: She weighs 25 bags from a normal morning. The average is 1,007.08 g.

panel.heading: Ruth's 1 kg bags of yam flour
items: Cpk 0.74: target too close to 1,000 g

say: Her spreadsheet's standard deviation, the typical distance from the average, is 3.21 g.

panel.heading: Ruth's 1 kg bags of yam flour
items: Cpk 0.74: target too close to 1,000 g

say: Cp compares the spread with the specification. Hers is 1.56, so the spread would fit if it were centred.

panel.heading: Ruth's 1 kg bags of yam flour
items: Cpk 0.74: target too close to 1,000 g

say: But Cpk, which checks the nearer limit, is only 0.74. Her target sits too close to 1,000 g, so some underweight bags are expected.
Moving the target to 1,012 g lifts Cpk to 1.25. A fixed-volume scoop and a fine top-up spoon is the cheaper long-term fix. And 25 values is only a first look.

panel.heading: Ruth's 1 kg bags of yam flour
items: Cpk 0.74: target too close to 1,000 g
panel.rule: Never fix underweight by guessing. Raise the target first.

say: A pilot run is a full-size batch under real conditions, before you promise volume. Write its purpose and pass criteria in numbers, such as yield at least 83%.

panel.heading: Write the plan before the day

say: Give roles. One person, often you, only watches and times.

panel.heading: Write the plan before the day

say: Record times, temperatures and weights, and agree stop rules, like oil smoking. Then do a first-article check: inspect the first few items against every point before making the rest.

panel.heading: Write the plan before the day

say: Kemi pilots three 9 kg loads. The first-article check catches thick dough on load 1. Load 2 goes to plan. On load 3, Tolu rushes and almost doubles the wok load. The oil cools and the chin-chin turns pale and oily.

panel.heading: Fix and repeat, not go
right: A marked bowl for each wok load

say: In a same-day debrief she asks what we planned, what happened, why, and what we will change. She adds a marked bowl and a timer, changing one thing at a time.
Only after three loads in a row pass does she accept the order.

panel.heading: Fix and repeat, not go
right: A marked bowl for each wok load

say: To remember. Weigh and use percentages. Measure yield and losses. Work backwards from the order. Check your spread and your centre. And go only when several pilot runs in a row pass.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Formula percentages are your product's identity
Work backwards from packs to flour
Low Cpk: move target; low Cp: reduce spread
Go only after several passing runs

say: Your turn. Build a scale-up sheet from a weighed batch, measure 25 items and work out Cp and Cpk, then plan and run a pilot with a debrief.
